title: To save its manufacturing base, Europe needs to look east
gist: Germany's 'China Shock 2.0' — rising Chinese imports of cars and machinery alongside falling Chinese demand for German exports — threatens to drag down Central and Eastern Europe's manufacturing base, which is heavily dependent on German demand and investment (German FDI to CEE fell 22.5% in 2022-24, greenfield pledges down two-thirds). Domestic consumption has bought CEE time, but the author argues the region must push for local-content requirements in emerging EU safeguards so reshoring lands in CEE.

insights.claim: Paris, Brussels and Berlin are in a rare moment of alignment on the need for protectionist measures against Chinese overcapacity.
insights.so_what: Raises the probability of EU safeguards/tariffs on Chinese cars, capital goods and machinery — negative for Chinese exporters, supportive for EU-based producers.
insights.quote: Paris, Brussels, and Berlin find themselves in a rare moment of alignment on the need for protectionist measures against Chinese overcapacity.
insights.locator: Something is stirring in EU trade policy
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Chinese imports of cars, capital goods and industrial machinery into Germany are rising rapidly while Chinese demand for these same EU exports is declining, leading to job cuts and calls for safeguards.
insights.so_what: Double squeeze on German industrial champions' core segments; even free-traders now see a 'China Shock 2.0'.
insights.quote: even stubborn supporters of free trade are increasingly convinced that German manufacturing faces a China Shock 2.0
insights.locator: In recent months, Germany’s malaise has morphed
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Germany's economy is weighed down by the cutoff of Russian energy, transatlantic uncertainty and declining Chinese demand; its meager growth has come from consumption and government spending while exports have been falling.
insights.so_what: Export-led weakness in Germany transmits directly to supplier economies in CEE.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Industry accounts for 21 to 33 percent of national GDP across Central and Eastern Europe, giving Europe an internal production platform that could make reshoring credible.
insights.so_what: CEE is the natural location for any EU reshoring push away from China.
insights.locator: Something is stirring in EU trade policy
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: EU investors own about 85 percent of FDI stock in CEE, yet FDI from Germany fell 22.5 percent between 2022 and 2024 and has not recovered; French and other investors have only partly offset it.
insights.so_what: Capital formation in CEE manufacturing is weakening, threatening future capacity and growth.
insights.quote: FDI from Germany fell by 22.5 percent between 2022 and 2024 and has not recovered since
insights.locator: For CEE, this should be a warning
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Czechia and Slovakia are the most exposed: Czechia sends 32 percent of exports to Germany and a sixth of its exporters serve no other market; Slovakia's exports approach 90 percent of GDP with autos at 34 percent of exports.
insights.so_what: Czech and Slovak growth, currencies and assets are most sensitive to the erosion of Europe's automotive position.
insights.locator: Czechia and Slovakia are the most exposed
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Germany's share of CEE countries' exports has fallen only one to three percentage points since 2018; in 2024 Germany still took 27.1 percent of Polish and 24.9 percent of Hungarian exports, 20.5 percent of Romanian and 15.2 percent of Bulgarian exports.
insights.so_what: Diversification away from Germany has been minimal, so the German slowdown will propagate across the region.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Austria is an important destination for industrial inputs and an anchor for banking and services in Slovenia, Croatia and the Balkans, often their top investor.
insights.so_what: Balkan economies carry indirect exposure via the German-Austrian value chain and Austrian banks.
insights.locator: This pattern extends beyond CEE’s core four
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: If the German-anchored model continues to falter, what began as a slowdown in Germany could tip parts of CEE into severe recession.
insights.so_what: Tail risk of CEE recession — relevant for regional equities, banks and sovereign credit.
insights.quote: what began as a slowdown in Germany could tip parts of CEE into severe recession
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Early symptoms are visible: industrial output in Hungary and Slovakia contracted throughout 2025, while Romania ran a 9.3 percent of GDP budget deficit in 2024, the largest in the EU.
insights.so_what: Romania's fiscal position is a distinct vulnerability; Hungary and Slovakia show industrial contagion already underway.
insights.locator: The question is how much time
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Poland grew around 3.6 percent in 2025 on rising real wages, robust domestic demand and EU funds absorption, and has overtaken China as Germany's fourth-largest import source.
insights.so_what: Poland is the relative outperformer, with consumption-led growth less exposed to German exports.
insights.locator: So far, CEE economies have managed
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Exporters are diversifying, with double-digit growth in exports to intra-CEE markets, the UK (less reliable given its openness to Chinese cars) and the US (harder because of tariffs).
insights.so_what: Diversification is real but constrained by tariffs and Chinese competition in third markets.
insights.locator: Exporters have also made a genuine effort
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Domestic consumption only buys time: German firms are cutting expensive domestic capacity first, but cheaper CEE plants will not be protected forever, and greenfield investment pledges are down two-thirds.
insights.so_what: Second-order risk: CEE plant closures follow German cuts with a lag; future capacity is already being hollowed out.
insights.quote: While German firms are cutting expensive domestic capacity first, cheaper CEE plants will not be protected forever.
insights.locator: But domestic consumption can only buy
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Germany's €500 billion infrastructure fund will add demand for raw materials and machinery, but only 65 percent of its allocation was disbursed in 2025, so its support for CEE will be limited.
insights.so_what: German fiscal stimulus is underdelivering; don't count on it to rescue regional manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Defense spending is unlikely to anchor manufacturing: even at 3.5 percent of GDP only a fraction goes to equipment, too little for a manufacturing sector that is one-fifth of the German economy.
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the consensus that rearmament will offset industrial decline in Germany.
insights.quote: Defense spending is also unlikely to provide a new anchor.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

themes.theme: CEE strategy in EU industrial policy

insights.claim: Polish PM Donald Tusk's declared year of 'turbo acceleration' rings hollow given inevitable knock-on effects, while Hungary's new government has taken a welcome collaborative stance.
insights.so_what: Skepticism toward Polish growth optimism; Hungarian policy shift may ease EU coordination.
insights.locator: The knock-on effects of Germany’s China Shock
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The new Rhine Group growth task force of Western European thinkers failed to include proper CEE representation despite CEE being the EU's fastest-growing region.
insights.so_what: Signals risk that EU industrial policy is designed around Western European interests.
insights.locator: Still, regional capitals need a more coherent
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Rather than dismantling the EU emissions trading scheme, CEE should work within a loosened scheme and use the incoming Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism to level the playing field against cheap Chinese goods.
insights.so_what: Expect ETS loosening rather than abolition, and CBAM increasingly framed as a trade-defense tool.
insights.locator: CEE has at times formed a somewhat united front
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: CEE capitals should insist that EU subsidies and safeguards include local content requirements strong enough to ensure onshoring lands in the region's manufacturing base; without CEE, European reshoring cannot deliver a China-proof industrial strategy.
insights.so_what: Local-content rules would favor CEE-based production and suppliers in any EU reshoring push.
insights.quote: without CEE, European reshoring will struggle to deliver on its promise of a China-proof industrial strategy
insights.locator: As Paris, Berlin, and Brussels converge
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
